commands.tooltip: Prints the version of the Ollama binary, useful when reading docs that assume a minimum release or troubleshooting odd behaviour. The same info appears at the end of `ollama serve` startup logs. Pair with `ollama ls` to confirm the daemon is reachable.

Shows every model you have pulled, with its tag (a version label like 3b or latest), size, and modification time. `ls` is an alias for `ollama list`. New models arrive with `ollama pull`, and `ollama ps` shows only the ones currently loaded in memory.

Downloads the default llama3.2 tag from the Ollama registry to your machine, where it stays for offline use. The first run of a model also triggers this download automatically. Add a tag like llama3.2:3b to grab a specific size variant.

Fetches the 3 billion parameter llama3.2 variant, a lighter model that runs comfortably on CPU-only laptops and 4-6 GB GPUs. The tag after the colon selects the size or quantization (compressed precision) of the same base model. Compare with llama3.2:1b for an even faster, dumber model.

Gets the 1 billion parameter llama3.2 build, the fastest and lightest official variant, usable on very modest hardware. It is best for quick tests, classification, and prototyping rather than serious writing. `ollama show llama3.2:1b` reveals its exact size after the pull.

Starts an interactive chat session with the llama3.2 model: you type prompts, the model replies, and the conversation history is kept in context. Type /bye or press Ctrl-D to exit, /help lists more slash commands, and /set changes session options. For a single question, pass the prompt as an argument instead.

commands.cmd: ollama run llama3.2 'Write a haiku about Linux'
commands.desc: Ask a model a single question
commands.tooltip: Runs one prompt through llama3.2 and prints only the reply, then exits, which is ideal for scripts and shell pipelines. Wrap the prompt in quotes so the shell treats it as one argument. The interactive alternative is `ollama run llama3.2` with no prompt.

commands.cmd: ollama run llama3.2 'Return a JSON list of three colors' --format json
commands.tooltip: Forces llama3.2 to answer in valid JSON, matching the schema implied by the prompt, which is handy for feeding results into jq or other programs. The --format flag constrains the model to structured output instead of free text. Pair with `curl http://localhost:11434/api/generate` for the same behaviour over HTTP.

Permanently removes the llama3.2 model files from your Ollama storage directory, freeing several gigabytes. There is no undo, and the model must be downloaded again with `ollama pull llama3.2` if you change your mind. Run `ollama ls` first to confirm which tag you are deleting.

Lists the models Ollama has loaded into memory right now, with their size, how long they have been resident, and how much VRAM or RAM they occupy. A model stays loaded for a few minutes after its last request unless `ollama stop` is used. This is the first place to look when a model feels slow or memory is tight.

Forces Ollama to unload llama3.2 from RAM or VRAM immediately, freeing memory that idle models otherwise hold for several minutes. The model stays on disk, so the next request reloads it with a small delay. Use `ollama ps` afterwards to confirm it is gone.

Prints metadata for llama3.2: parameter count, quantization level, context length, license, and the architecture it runs on. It is the quick way to check whether a pulled model matches your hardware before running it. Add --modelfile to see the exact build recipe.

Displays the Modelfile (the recipe of base model, prompt template, parameters, and system message) that defines llama3.2. This is the same content `ollama create` consumes, so it is a great starting point for building your own tuned variant. Related: `ollama show llama3.2 --parameters`.

commands.desc: Clone a model under a new name
commands.tooltip: Creates a local copy of llama3.2 named my-llama-copy without downloading anything again, since Ollama stores shared blobs once. Use it to experiment safely with `ollama create` modifications or to give a tuned model a stable name. Delete the copy with `ollama rm my-llama-copy`.

commands.desc: Build a custom model from a Modelfile
commands.tooltip: Assembles a new model called mymodel from the instructions in Modelfile, which typically starts with FROM llama3.2 and adds a custom system prompt, temperature, or template. The file lives in the current directory unless -f points elsewhere. Tweak and recreate the same name to iterate, and `ollama show mymodel --modelfile` to inspect the result.

Builds mymodel from Modelfile while quantizing the weights to q4_K_M, a 4-bit format that shrinks memory use and speeds up CPU inference at a small accuracy cost. The -q flag only works when the Modelfile imports a source model, not for imported GGUF files. q4_K_M is a solid default; q8_0 trades size for fidelity.

commands.desc: Upload a model to a registry
commands.tooltip: Uploads myuser/mymodel to a remote Ollama registry so other machines or people can `ollama pull` it. The namespace must be an account you own on ollama.com or a private registry, and you must be signed in first with `ollama signin`. Private registries need the --insecure flag when they lack TLS.

Authenticates with ollama.com so you can push models you created with `ollama create` to your namespace. It opens a browser flow or prompts for credentials in the terminal. `ollama signout` removes the saved session.

commands.desc: Run Ollama with a custom model directory
commands.tooltip: Starts the Ollama server with its model storage redirected from the default ~/.ollama/models to /data/ollama, useful on machines where the home partition is small or models should live on a big data drive. Set the variable per-command or export it in your shell profile. `ollama serve` alone uses the defaults; the server listens on 127.0.0.1:11434.

commands.desc: List local models via the API
commands.tooltip: Queries the Ollama REST API on port 11434 and prints every locally stored model as JSON, with name, size, and modification time. It is the API equivalent of `ollama ls`, useful from scripts or when no ollama binary exists on the machine. Pipe through `python3 -m json.tool` to pretty-print.

commands.desc: List loaded models via the API
commands.tooltip: Hits the Ollama REST API to show which models are currently resident in memory, mirroring `ollama ps` but returning JSON that scripts can parse. Each entry includes the model name and how long it has been loaded. Use `ollama stop` or the API to unload a model.

commands.desc: Send a chat request to Ollama's API
commands.tooltip: Sends a single chat message to the running Ollama server over HTTP, with the conversation passed as a messages array exactly like OpenAI's API shape. Add "stream":false to get the full reply in one JSON response instead of tokens as they are generated. This is how other programs talk to Ollama; `ollama run llama3.2` is the interactive shortcut.

commands.cmd: curl -s http://localhost:11434/api/generate -d '{"model":"llama3.2","prompt":"Explain Docker in one sentence","stream":false}'
commands.tooltip: Asks the Ollama server to complete a raw prompt, without chat history, and returns JSON containing the response field. stream:false makes the server buffer the whole answer instead of streaming token chunks. The companion endpoint /api/chat handles conversational messages; both speak to the server started by `ollama serve`.

commands.desc: Log in to Hugging Face interactively
commands.tooltip: Stores a Hugging Face access token in ~/.cache/huggingface/token so `hf download` and `hf upload` can reach gated or private repos. It opens a browser to create the token, or accepts a pasted token at the prompt. Generate tokens at huggingface.co/settings/tokens; `hf auth whoami` confirms the logged-in account.

commands.desc: Log in with a token variable
commands.tooltip: Logs in non-interactively using the token stored in the HF_TOKEN environment variable, perfect for CI machines and scripts that cannot open a browser. The variable is single-quoted-safe because the shell expands it before hf runs. Add --add-to-git-credential to also let plain git commands authenticate.

commands.desc: Remove the saved Hugging Face token
commands.tooltip: Deletes the locally stored Hugging Face access token, so subsequent downloads of gated models will prompt again. Use it when rotating credentials or before handing a machine to someone else. `hf auth whoami` will then report that you are not logged in.

commands.desc: Show the logged-in Hugging Face account
commands.tooltip: Prints the username of the Hugging Face account whose token is stored locally, plus any org memberships. It is the fastest sanity check that authentication is working before downloading a gated model. Related: `hf auth list` shows every saved token.

Shows every Hugging Face token saved on this machine with its name and creation date, which is handy when several accounts or CI tokens are in play. Tokens are stored in ~/.cache/huggingface. Switch the active one with `hf auth switch`; delete with `hf auth logout`.

commands.desc: Print the current token to stdout
commands.tooltip: Outputs the active Hugging Face access token in plain text, useful for scripting but a security risk if the terminal is shared or the output is logged. Treat the printed value like a password. Prefer `hf auth whoami` when you only need to verify identity.

Lets you pick which saved Hugging Face token is active for the current user, without re-pasting tokens. Handy on machines shared between personal and work accounts. `hf auth list` shows what is available to switch between.

commands.desc: Download a model from the Hub
commands.tooltip: Downloads every file of the meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct repo into the Hugging Face cache, keyed by the repo name and revision so re-downloads are skipped. A model ID is the owner/repo-name pair from huggingface.co, like meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Gated models require `hf auth login` first, and --local-dir places files in a plain folder instead of the cache.

Fetches just the .safetensors weight files from the model repo, skipping tokenizers and configs, which saves bandwidth on big repos. The --include flag takes shell-style glob patterns and can be repeated. Add --exclude to filter further, or download individual files by naming them after the repo.

commands.desc: Download a model to a plain folder
commands.tooltip: Saves the all-MiniLM-L6-v2 embedding model directly under ./minilm instead of the hashed cache layout, mirroring how the repo looks on the Hub. A local-dir download is a copy, so deleting the folder removes the files but not the cache. Useful when a tool expects a model path rather than a model ID.

Fetches just the Q4_K_M GGUF file of the Llama-3.2-1B model into ./llama32. GGUF is a quantized (compressed) model format designed for CPU inference, and Q4_K_M is the popular quality/size sweet spot. Ollama-style runners and llama.cpp load these files directly, so this is how you fetch a model for CPU-only setups.

commands.desc: Upload a file to the Hub
commands.tooltip: Pushes model.safetensors to the myuser/my-repo repository on Hugging Face, committing it in a single shot. The repo must already exist (see `hf repos create`) or be created with --private, and you must be logged in as its owner. Repeat with more paths or a folder to upload several files at once.

commands.desc: Upload and create a private repo
commands.tooltip: Creates the private repo myuser/new-repo if it does not exist, then uploads model.safetensors into it in one command. Private repos are only visible to you and people you explicitly grant access to. Remove --private for a public upload.

commands.desc: Upload a large folder with resume
commands.tooltip: Uploads the whole model-weights directory to the Hub in chunks that survive network drops, designed for multi-gigabyte model directories. Unlike plain `hf upload`, an interrupted run can be resumed rather than restarted. Run it in a terminal that stays open, or use --token for unattended jobs.

Creates an empty repository named my-llm of type model on your Hugging Face account, ready for `hf upload`. The --type flag switches between model, dataset, and space. Add --private to keep it hidden, and --exist-ok to avoid errors if it already exists.

Makes a new model repository that only you can see, for work-in-progress weights or proprietary data. The --private flag can be flipped later with `hf repos settings`. Public repos are the default, so remember this flag when the model must not leak.

Permanently removes the entire myuser/old-model repository, including every file, revision, and commit history on Hugging Face. There is no trash bin, so download anything you need first. Consider `hf repos move` instead when the goal is just renaming.

Updates repository settings, here switching myuser/my-repo from public to private, which hides it from search and anonymous downloads. Existing downloaders keep their cached copies. Related flags: --public to reverse it and --protected for Spaces.

commands.desc: Transfer a repo to another namespace
commands.tooltip: Moves a model repository to a different owner namespace, typically your own org, preserving all history and URLs redirect automatically. You must have write access to both namespaces. The old name stops working once the move completes.

commands.desc: Inspect the Hugging Face download cache
commands.tooltip: Shows every repo cached locally with its size and the revisions held, giving you a picture of how much disk space models occupy. This is the 1.x replacement for the old scan-cache command. Free space with `hf cache rm` or `hf cache prune`.

commands.desc: Remove a repo from the cache
commands.tooltip: Deletes the cached files of the gpt2 model (which lives in the model namespace) from ~/.cache/huggingface, reclaiming its disk space. The model can always be re-downloaded with `hf download`. Use `hf cache ls` first to see what is cached and how big each repo is.

Deletes cached revisions no longer referenced by any tag or branch, the leftovers of repeated `hf download` calls that accumulate silently. It never touches the revision currently pointed at by a tag. Run `hf cache ls` before and after to see the reclaimed space.

Dumps the environment report used for Hugging Face bug reports: hf version, Python version, OS, token location, and whether a token is saved. Paste its output into a GitHub issue when something misbehaves. `hf version` prints just the version number for quick checks.

Prints the installed huggingface_hub version, which determines which subcommands and flags are available. Docs and error messages often assume a minimum version. Update with `pip install -U huggingface_hub`.

commands.desc: Show metadata for a Hub model
commands.tooltip: Prints metadata about the model repo: downloads, likes, license, tags, and the files it contains, without downloading anything. It is the CLI version of a model card page. Related: `hf models ls` searches the Hub and `hf download` fetches the files.

Lists the ten most-downloaded models on Hugging Face, sorted by the downloads counter, handy for discovering what the community actually uses. Add a search term as a positional argument, or --filter for tags like text-generation. `hf datasets ls` works the same way for datasets.

The old pre-1.x name for Hugging Face authentication, which now prints a deprecation warning and does nothing, because the CLI was renamed to `hf`. Run `hf auth login` instead for the same behaviour. Scripts still calling huggingface-cli should be migrated.

commands.desc: Serve a model with an OpenAI API
commands.tooltip: Starts a vLLM inference server exposing the model behind an OpenAI-compatible API on http://localhost:8000, with endpoints like /v1/chat/completions and /v1/models. The model ID is a Hugging Face repo name and is downloaded on first start, which can take a while. Swap in any other repo name to serve a different model.

Runs the Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 model on port 8001 instead of the default 8000, letting several vLLM servers share one machine. Point clients at http://localhost:8001/v1 and set their base_url accordingly. Use --host 0.0.0.0 to accept connections from other machines.

commands.desc: Expose the API on all interfaces
commands.tooltip: Binds the vLLM server to every network interface so other machines on the network can reach the OpenAI-compatible API. Anyone who can connect can use the model, so add --api-key or a firewall rule in untrusted networks. Default is localhost only.

Limits the model's context window to 8192 tokens, trading longer inputs for lower memory use and faster prefill. Long prompts that exceed the limit are rejected instead of silently truncated. Reduce it further when VRAM is tight; raise it when memory allows.

commands.desc: Use most of the GPU memory
commands.tooltip: Lets vLLM consume up to 90 percent of GPU memory for the KV cache, the buffer that stores conversation context, instead of the conservative default. Raise it on dedicated inference boxes to fit longer contexts; lower it when the GPU also runs other workloads. Combined with --max-model-len it is the main VRAM tuning knob.

Loads the AWQ-quantized Llama-2-7B weights with the matching --quantization awq flag, which vLLM needs because quantized files are not self-describing. AWQ (Activation-aware Weight Quantization) shrinks the model to 4-bit precision for lower VRAM use. The quantization value must match how the repo's weights were produced.

commands.desc: Shard the model across two GPUs
commands.tooltip: Splits the model across two GPUs with tensor parallelism, letting you serve models too large for one card. Each GPU holds half the weights and they cooperate on every forward pass. Requires GPUs on the same machine or fast interconnect, and a model with enough parameters to justify it.

commands.desc: Rename the model in the API
commands.tooltip: Makes the server answer to the name my-llama in /v1/models and requests, while actually running Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct underneath. Clients then pass "model": "my-llama" in their requests. Useful for stable names across model upgrades or for hiding which weights you run.

commands.desc: Require an API key for requests
commands.tooltip: Protects the OpenAI-compatible endpoints with a bearer token: clients must send "Authorization: Bearer sk-my-secret-key" or requests are rejected with 401. Choose a long random key, since anyone who has it can use the model. The same key also gates /health and metrics.

Forces the model to run in float16 (half precision), halving memory use versus fp32 with negligible quality loss on modern GPUs. vLLM usually auto-detects a good dtype, so this flag mainly resolves mismatches with unusual weight formats. For quantized weights, prefer --quantization instead.

Turns on function-calling support so the model can emit structured tool calls, with hermes telling vLLM how to parse this model family's output format. Clients then send tools in the chat request and receive tool_calls in the reply. The parser name must match the model's training format or parsing breaks.

commands.desc: Serve with a custom chat template
commands.tooltip: Uses the Jinja2 template in chat_template.jinja to format chat messages into the model's expected prompt shape, overriding the template bundled with the tokenizer. Custom templates fix garbled multi-turn output for models with unusual chat formats. Test with one /v1/chat/completions call after starting.

Limits how many sequences vLLM processes at once to 32, trading throughput for lower latency variance and predictable memory use. Each in-flight request holds KV cache space, so the cap matters when context windows are long. Raise it for chat workloads with many parallel users.

Asks the running vLLM server which model IDs it serves, printing each one through jq for clean output. The response mirrors OpenAI's /v1/models shape. The model id shown is what clients must pass as "model" in requests, especially after --served-model-name renames it.

Calls vLLM's chat endpoint with one user message, exactly like OpenAI's API, and prints the assistant's reply as JSON. The messages array carries the whole conversation history on multi-turn calls. Add "stream":true to receive tokens incrementally instead of one big response.

commands.cmd: curl -s http://localhost:8000/v1/completions -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"model":"meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct","prompt":"Once upon a time"}'
commands.desc: Send a raw text completion request
commands.tooltip: Uses the completions endpoint for raw prompt continuation without chat formatting, ideal for testing base models or non-chat tasks. The response contains the generated text plus token counts in usage. Chat models usually behave better through /v1/chat/completions, which applies their trained template.

Returns HTTP 200 with the body OK when the vLLM server and its engine are healthy, making it the endpoint load balancers and monitoring poll. A 503 means the engine died or is still starting. The first health check may stay non-OK for minutes while the model loads.

Sends text to the embeddings endpoint and receives a vector per input, ready for semantic search or clustering. The served model must be an embedding model like bge-small-en-v1.5, not a chat model. Response vectors appear under data[0].embedding, often truncated by the terminal, so pipe to a file.

Transcribes audio.mp3 with the base Whisper model, auto-detecting the language and printing a timestamped transcript while writing .txt, .vtt, .srt, .tsv, and .json files next to the audio. Model sizes tiny, base, small, medium, large-v3 trade speed against accuracy. The first run downloads the model weights automatically.

Transcribes Spanish audio using the small model, with --language skipping the auto-detection step and forcing Spanish decoding. Language codes follow ISO 639-1 (es, fr, de, ja, and so on). Forcing the language prevents misdetection on short clips and slightly speeds things up.

Transcribes audio.mp3 with the medium model and writes only plain-text transcripts into ./transcripts, keeping your working directory clean. --output_format picks between txt, vtt, srt, tsv, json, jsonl, or all. The output filename mirrors the input name, so audio.mp3 becomes audio.txt.

Transcribes any-language audio and translates the result into English, one pass, no intermediate files needed. The --task flag switches between transcribe and translate; only English output is supported. Combine with --language to pin the source language instead of auto-detecting.

Disables fp16 (half-precision) inference so the tiny model runs in fp32 on CPUs without CUDA, avoiding errors on machines without an NVIDIA GPU. GPU users keep the default fp16 for speed. Add --device cpu explicitly on systems where CUDA is broken or absent.

Adds start and end time for every word to the JSON transcript, enabling highlight-style captions and forced alignment. Timestamps become far more granular than the default segment-level ones. The word data only appears in JSON or TSV output, not plain text.

commands.cmd: whisper audio.mp3 --model base --initial_prompt 'This is a technical podcast about Linux'
commands.tooltip: Seeds the decoder with a hint about the audio's style and vocabulary, which often fixes repeated hallucinations and improves spelling of domain terms. Whisper weighs the prompt's style more than its exact words. Useful for names, jargon, and accented speech that default transcription mangles.

Transcribes English audio with the large-v3 model and writes an .srt subtitle file with segment timings, ready for video players or caption pipelines. SRT is the format most players and editors accept. Large-v3 is the most accurate Whisper model but slowest, so reserve it for clean, important audio.

Runs beam search with a width of 5 instead of the greedy default, exploring several candidate transcripts and keeping the most probable one. Higher beam sizes improve accuracy on hard audio at a real speed cost. Values of 5 are a common sweet spot; the default is 1 (greedy).

Produces txt, vtt, srt, tsv, json, and jsonl outputs for the same audio into ./transcripts in one pass, so you get plain text, subtitles, and timestamps without re-transcribing. This is the default behaviour when no output_format is given. Later runs overwrite these files.

Runs the lm-evaluation-harness on the MMLU benchmark with the model loaded via Hugging Face transformers, giving 5 example answers per question (few-shot) before scoring. The pretrained= value is a Hugging Face model ID. Runs are long and download model weights first; expect many minutes to hours depending on GPU.

commands.desc: Evaluate on TruthfulQA with a device
commands.tooltip: Scores the model on truthfulqa_mc2, a benchmark measuring whether answers are both true and informative, while pinning inference to GPU 0 with --device cuda:0. Use --device cpu to force CPU execution on machines without CUDA. Results print as a table with acc and other metrics per task.

Evaluates hellaswag using vLLM as the inference engine, which is dramatically faster than the transformers backend on big models. --model_args takes comma-separated key=value settings, here passing tensor_parallel_size=1. vLLM must be installed (`pip install vllm`) and the harness's vllm extra enabled.

Runs the GSM8K math benchmark with --apply_chat_template so prompts are formatted as chat turns, matching how instruct-tuned models were trained instead of raw text. Skipping this flag tanks scores on chat models. Add --num_fewshot 8 for the standard GSM8K few-shot setup.

Evaluates only the first 100 hellaswag examples, cutting a long run down to minutes so you can verify the setup before committing to the full benchmark. The limit accepts a fraction too, like 0.1. Remove --limit for the real, complete evaluation.

Writes the evaluation results JSON into ./results/ and, with --log_samples, also saves every individual prompt and model answer for post-hoc analysis. Saved samples let you audit failures and recompute metrics offline. Without --log_samples only aggregated scores are stored.

commands.desc: Run evaluation from a YAML config
commands.tooltip: Loads model, batch, and generation settings from my_eval_config.yaml, keeping long flag lists out of the command line and making runs reproducible. Settings given directly on the command line override the file. Great for re-running the same benchmark after model changes.

Prints all task, group, subtask, and tag names the harness knows, which is the first stop when picking a --tasks value. Group names like mmlu evaluate a whole family of subtasks at once. Individual subtask names end with a topic, for example mmlu_anatomy.

Shows only the top-level task groups (mmlu, hellaswag, glue, and so on), which evaluate several related subtasks and report an aggregated score. Passing a group name to --tasks runs every subtask inside it. Related: `lm-eval ls subtasks` and `lm-eval ls tags`.

Checks that the hellaswag task definition loads and its few-shot prompt construction works, catching YAML or data errors before a long evaluation run starts. It is the harness's self-test for task configs. Custom tasks can be added with --include_path pointing at their directory.

Validates my_custom_task defined in the local ./custom_tasks directory, which is where your own YAML task definitions live. This catches config mistakes without burning GPU time. Once it passes, use the same --include_path with `lm-eval run` to evaluate on the task.

commands.desc: OCR an image to a text file
commands.tooltip: Runs OCR (optical character recognition) on image.png and writes the recognized text to output.txt in the current directory. The second argument is the output base name; tesseract appends the extension. Install language data with apt for non-English input, and use --psm to tune page layout.

commands.desc: Print OCR text to the terminal
commands.tooltip: Writes the recognized text straight to stdout instead of a file, perfect for piping into grep, wc, or a script. The special output name stdout is a tesseract convention; a lone dash also works. Redirect with > to save the result to a file of your choosing.

Recognizes Spanish text using the spa language pack, which must be installed first (apt package tesseract-ocr-spa on Debian systems). The -l flag accepts any installed language code. `tesseract --list-langs` shows which packs you actually have.

Recognizes English and Spanish in the same image by joining language codes with a plus sign, letting tesseract pick per-word. Add more languages the same way, though each one slows recognition slightly. Requires every listed language pack to be installed.

Prints every language pack tesseract can currently use, from the tessdata directory it was built against. Seeing only eng and osd means only English is installed. Language packs are separate packages, like tesseract-ocr-fra for French on Debian systems.

Tells tesseract the image is a uniform block of text (PSM 6), which fixes garbled output on clean single-column scans. Page segmentation modes 0-13 describe layouts from sparse text to a single word or character. Use --help-psm to see every mode explained.

Selects OCR engine mode 1, the neural LSTM engine, versus the legacy engine (mode 0) or tesseract's auto-choice (mode 3). The LSTM engine is far more accurate on modern fonts. Modes only matter when your build ships both engines.

Tells tesseract the scan is 300 DPI, which matters for low-resolution images where tesseract underestimates text size and fails to find lines. When no DPI is embedded, tesseract guesses and warns about it. 300 is the standard scan resolution.

Limits recognition to the whitelisted characters, here digits only, which eliminates letters in numeric-only images like barcodes or account numbers. The -c flag sets a tesseract config variable directly on the command line. Add letters by extending the list.

Wraps the recognized text as an invisible layer over the original image in a PDF, so the file stays visually identical but text can be searched and copied. The output base name gains the .pdf extension. Great for archival scans that need to be findable.

Prints the tesseract version, the bundled Leptonica library version, and build features like the available engines. Docs and troubleshooting guides often ask for this output. The 5.x line uses the LSTM engine by default.

Launches the ComfyUI web server from its installation directory, serving the node-based UI at http://127.0.0.1:8188. First start downloads or compiles nothing but requires PyTorch and the requirements.txt packages installed. Keep the terminal open; Ctrl-C stops the server.

commands.desc: Start ComfyUI on a custom port
commands.tooltip: Runs the ComfyUI server on port 8189 instead of the default 8188, useful when the port is taken or several instances must coexist. Point your browser at http://127.0.0.1:8189 afterwards. The port matters when scripts hardcode the API base URL.

Binds the ComfyUI server to all interfaces so other machines can open the UI and submit workflows, but also lets anyone on the network run arbitrary Python through custom nodes, which is effectively remote code execution. Only do this on trusted networks, ideally behind a reverse proxy with authentication. The default --listen 127.0.0.1 stays local-only.

Forces every model to run on the CPU, which works but is dramatically slower, mainly for machines without CUDA or ROCm support. Text-encoder-only steps stay tolerable; diffusion sampling can take minutes per image. Check whether your hardware really lacks GPU support before resorting to this.

commands.desc: Open the UI in a browser on start
commands.tooltip: Automatically opens the ComfyUI web UI in your default browser once the server is ready, saving a manual tab. Mostly a convenience for desktop use; headless servers should omit it. Pair with --port to control which URL opens.

Writes all generated images and videos to /data/comfy-outputs instead of the default output folder inside the ComfyUI directory. Handy when the install lives on a small system drive and results should land on a big data disk. The queue and history still track the files by their new paths.

Disables CUDA's async memory pool, working around CUDA out-of-memory crashes on some drivers and cards, at a small performance cost. ComfyUI prints a warning hinting at this flag when it suspects cudaMallocAsync is the culprit. Older torch builds may need it more often.

Unloads models back to system RAM between nodes instead of keeping them on the GPU, letting 6 GB cards run SDXL-sized workloads by trading speed. ComfyUI 4.x defaults to dynamic VRAM management, so this flag mainly helps on cards it misjudges. Expect slower iterations but fewer out-of-memory errors.

Returns JSON with ComfyUI's version, Python version, GPU details, and current RAM/VRAM usage, the standard health check for a running server. A connection refused error means ComfyUI is not running. Related endpoints: /queue for job status and /object_info for the node catalogue.

Shows the pending and running workflow jobs as readable JSON, with each job's node graph and prompt id. The queue fills up as clients submit workflows while the server is busy. Cancel pending jobs by POSTing to /queue with a delete list, or interrupt the running job separately.

Aborts the workflow currently executing, which is the ComfyUI equivalent of pressing stop in the UI. It interrupts generation mid-step; finished images stay on disk, and pending jobs in the queue still run afterwards. Use the /queue endpoint's delete action to clear waiting jobs too.

commands.cmd: curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8188/free -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"unload_models": true, "free_memory": true}'
commands.tooltip: Unloads loaded models from VRAM and frees cached memory, the recovery move after an out-of-memory error or before switching to a heavy workflow. The JSON body toggles model unloading and memory freeing independently. Retry your workflow after the VRAM drops.

Uploads photo.png into ComfyUI's input folder so workflows can reference it by filename, the API path behind img2img and inpainting jobs. The -F flags send multipart form fields: the file, the folder type, and overwrite behaviour. The response echoes the stored filename to use in your workflow JSON.

Fetches the full node catalogue and prints just the node class names, showing what custom nodes and built-ins the server can run. A workflow that references a missing class fails with class_type not found, so this is the check before installing new node packs. Each entry's JSON also documents its inputs.

Prints the version of comfy-cli, the official ComfyUI management tool that handles install, launch, and node/model management. The CLI auto-detects your ComfyUI workspace, falling back to ~/comfy/ComfyUI. Install or update it with `pipx install comfy-cli`.

Downloads ComfyUI, ComfyUI-Manager, and CUDA-enabled PyTorch into a default workspace, ready to launch with `comfy launch`. Swap --nvidia for --amd, --m-series, or --cpu to match your hardware. The install can take a while because PyTorch is large.

commands.desc: Start ComfyUI as a background daemon
commands.tooltip: Launches the ComfyUI server in the background and returns, so your terminal stays free, with the server reachable at http://127.0.0.1:8188. Stop it later with `comfy stop`. Pass extra server flags after --, like `comfy launch -- --port 8190`.

Shuts down the ComfyUI instance that `comfy launch --background` started, freeing GPU memory and the port. It targets the workspace daemon recorded by comfy-cli, so manually started servers need Ctrl-C in their own terminal. Verify with `curl http://127.0.0.1:8188/system_stats` failing afterwards.

Fetches the SDXL base checkpoint straight into ComfyUI's models/checkpoints directory, where the Load Checkpoint node finds it by filename. The --relative-path flag mirrors the models folder layout. CivitAI URLs work too, with --set-civitai-api-token for gated downloads.

Shows every model file in the workspace's models tree, grouped by folder like checkpoints, loras, and vae. Filenames here are the exact strings workflow nodes expect, so check before referencing a model in a workflow. Add --relative-path to filter one folder.

Installs the comfyui-controlnet-aux custom node pack (preprocessors for ControlNet workflows) into the workspace and its Python dependencies. Custom nodes extend ComfyUI with new node classes visible in /object_info. Replace the name with any pack from the registry; `comfy node update all` refreshes everything later.

Pulls the latest version of all installed custom node packs, which often fixes compatibility breaks after a ComfyUI core update. Updates occasionally change node inputs, so workflows may need re-exporting. Run `comfy update` first to bring ComfyUI itself up to date.

commands.desc: Install Ollama with the official script
commands.tooltip: Downloads and runs the official Ollama installer, which puts the binary in your path and sets up a systemd service on Linux. Piping a remote script into sh always carries risk, so review the script first if you are cautious. Afterwards `ollama run llama3.2` starts a chat and downloads the model on demand.

Installs the openai-whisper package and its dependencies, including PyTorch, which makes this a multi-gigabyte download on top of the small package itself. The `whisper` command-line tool arrives with it for transcribing audio. Prefer a virtual environment so PyTorch does not clash with system packages.

Installs faster-whisper, a CTranslate2-based reimplementation of Whisper that runs up to four times faster, but it ships no command-line tool: it is a Python library you import in your own scripts. The `whisper` CLI from openai-whisper or tools like WhisperX provide the terminal interface instead. The pip package pulls ctranslate2 and PyAV but not PyTorch.

Installs vLLM with CUDA support for serving LLMs, pulling in large dependencies like PyTorch, so expect a sizeable download. After install, `vllm serve` launches an OpenAI-compatible API server. CUDA must match your driver; vLLM wheels target recent NVIDIA driver versions.

Installs the lm-evaluation-harness package, which provides the `lm-eval` command for benchmarking language models on tasks like MMLU and hellaswag. The base install covers CPU evaluation; add extras for backends, for example `pip install lm-eval[hf]` or `pip install lm-eval[vllm]`, which pull torch or vLLM. PyPI's project name uses an underscore, but pip resolves lm-eval the same way.

commands.desc: Install the Hugging Face Hub CLI
commands.tooltip: Installs huggingface_hub, the Python library that also provides the `hf` command-line tool for downloading and uploading models. Version 1.x ships the hf binary; older releases called it huggingface-cli, which is now deprecated. Upgrade regularly with -U since subcommands evolve across minor versions.

Installs the CPU build of PyTorch by default, a large package that nearly every local ML tool depends on. For CUDA GPU support, follow the official install command for your CUDA version from pytorch.org instead, since pip's default build has no GPU acceleration. Use a virtual environment to avoid version conflicts with system Python.

commands.desc: Install the Hugging Face Transformers library
commands.tooltip: Installs transformers, the Python library for loading and running Hugging Face models, which is what tools like lm-eval use under the hood. It is a library, not a CLI, so commands go through other programs or short Python snippets. Requires torch or another backend to actually run models.

Installs the tesseract OCR engine plus the Spanish language pack, which `tesseract -l spa` needs; English (eng) ships with the main package. Add more packs like tesseract-ocr-fra for other languages. On Debian-based systems this is the standard install route.

Installs comfy-cli into an isolated environment via pipx, keeping it out of system Python and making the `comfy` command available. This is the recommended install method for the official ComfyUI lifecycle tool. First run may ask about analytics, which `comfy --skip-prompt tracking disable` turns off.

commands.desc: Convert a Whisper model for faster-whisper
commands.tooltip: Converts the original large-v3 Whisper weights into CTranslate2 format that faster-whisper loads, writing float16 weights into whisper-large-v3-ct2. The converter ships with the ctranslate2 package. Load the result by passing the output directory as the model path in faster-whisper.
